tests.method: Viewed full provided raster without reading identities, reports, or font source; compared RU UI 18px/400/14, RU and EN body 22px/400/18, RU and EN headings 48px/500/48, isolated diagnostic forms 54px at weights 100 and 900 / optical 64.

blind_assessment.confidence: high for the absence of an obvious line-level difference in this sheet; moderate for visual positioning
blind_assessment.condition: At the supplied raster size and the shown weight/optical-size combinations. This does not establish that outlines or rendering are identical.
blind_assessment.real_line_observation: The paired RU UI line, RU and EN body sentences, and RU and EN headings preserve effectively the same visible width, rhythm, color, openness, and word silhouettes. I cannot identify a repeatable character change across those lines.
blind_assessment.diagnostic_observation: B visibly gives capital I horizontal bars in the isolated Il1 sequences at the extreme weights. That is a useful identification cue, but it does not recur as a perceptible character change in the supplied real lines.
blind_assessment.brief_fit: Both look compact, clean, open in the regular text samples, and restrained rather than strongly expressive. The Cyrillic Л/л and Д/д have recognizable local forms. A moderately humanist reading is plausible from the softened rhythm, but the sheet alone does not establish a distinctive or self-contained Cyrillic voice.

verdict_scope: Shared visual verdicts for A and B on this sheet. Current-font SHA identifies the requested artifact but does not decode A/B. Headings pass means the shown headings are coherent and readable; it does not certify distinctive branding.

findings.specific: The repeated RU/EN lines do not reveal a stable A/B change in brand character.
findings.recommendation: Do not claim a proven line-level personality improvement from this matrix.
findings.acceptance_test: Use randomized, order-swapped unfamiliar RU/EN sentences with multiple occurrences of changed forms; collect preference and repeat identification across repeats before making a distinctiveness claim.

findings.specific: The serifed capital I in B is visible at both diagnostic extremes; surrounding line rhythm looks unchanged.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate it as an identification feature rather than evidence of a new overall voice.
findings.acceptance_test: Render real mixed-language names, identifiers, and UI labels containing I/l/1 at actual UI sizes and verify each character can be identified.

findings.specific: Both heading pairs have steady spacing and compatible Latin/Cyrillic color. The Cyrillic lower-case and cap shapes look native enough in the supplied words, but coverage is sparse.
findings.recommendation: Retain the restrained heading direction; broaden Cyrillic proofing before describing the design as self-contained.
findings.acceptance_test: Inspect paragraph and heading specimens with representative Cyrillic combinations, punctuation, numerals, and mixed scripts at regular and bold weights.

findings.specific: The specimen contains no paragraphs or sustained reading evidence.
findings.recommendation: Keep body and sustained-reading claims provisional.
findings.acceptance_test: Review multi-paragraph RU/EN text at intended body sizes and line lengths, then run actual reader testing if claiming reading comfort.

limits: No human participant results; no designer impersonation.
No A/B identity key or earlier/current reports read.
Only the supplied raster was visually assessed; no source fonts edited.
No paragraph reading, timing, print, low-resolution-device, or cross-platform tests.
No claim that the fonts are technically identical or that one letter establishes overall character.
